title: Descriptive statistics & visual data analysis
source: Session 2 handout (DDM 26/27) – Superstore exercises in Stata/Excel, Wurman (2000), Keim et al. (2010)
tagline: Before you model anything, you must know what kind of variable you have – the measurement scale decides which statistics and which charts are allowed. Then you summarise (central tendency, dispersion, correlation) and show it with the right graph.
goals: classify a variable as **nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio**
say which **question type** produces which kind of variable
pick the right measure of **central tendency and dispersion** for a scale
interpret a **Pearson correlation** and choose a fitting **chart**

sections.heading: Types of data and variables
sections.lead: Two families: non-metric (categorical) and metric (numerical). Each step to the right adds information – and allows more statistics.

steps.label: Nominal
points: gender, product category, region, purchase occasion

steps.label: Ordinal
steps.text: Categories with a hierarchy (order), distances unknown

steps.label: Interval
points: IQ, Likert scales (satisfaction, NPS, brand attitude)

blocks.text: Ratio test: does “0” mean **nothing at all** (0 € revenue)? Then it is ratio. 0 on a satisfaction scale does not mean “no satisfaction” → interval.

blocks.title: Good questionnaire design
items: Mostly **closed-ended** questions – more effective for quantitative data; the flow is fixed before the research
Clear language, brief and simple questions; follow a natural flow (train of thought, chronology)
Do **not lead** respondents to an answer
Opening: brief presentation of the research, anonymity and privacy, instructions
Content can cover facts, awareness, frequency of behaviour, opinions, motivations, intentions, attitudes, demographics & psychographics

head: Question type
Example
Variable produced
rows: “Have you ever visited our store?” Yes / No
“Which channels do you use?” (+ “don't know”, “other – specify”)
“I am satisfied …” strongly disagree → strongly agree; semantic differential or matrix

items.label: CSAT
items.text: How satisfied are customers with products/services? Scale 1–5.

items.label: NPS
items.text: How likely are you to recommend us? Scale 0–10.

items.label: CES
items.text: How easy was it to get an issue resolved, a request fulfilled, a product bought or returned? Scale 1–7.

blocks.name: Customer Satisfaction Score
blocks.formula: CSAT = (number of satisfied customers (4 and 5) / number of responses) × 100

blocks.name: Net Promoter Score
vars: Passives (7–8) count in the total but in neither group

blocks.name: Customer Effort Score
blocks.formula: CES = (number of customers answering 5, 6 or 7 / number of responses) × 100
blocks.note: Statement: “This company made it easy for me to handle my issue” (1 = strongly disagree … 7 = strongly agree).

sections.heading: Univariate statistics
sections.lead: Univariate analysis looks at one variable at a time.

items.text: How often a value occurs (**absolute**); divided by the number of observations → **relative** frequency (% of sample). Frequencies contain the whole information about a distribution.
Most common measure of central tendency; good summary of **metric** data, but sensitive to outliers.
The middle score once data are ordered by magnitude. **Not** computable for nominal variables.
The most frequent value – the highest bar of a histogram. Computable for **any** type of variable.
Average of the squared differences from the mean (metric variables).
Square root of the variance, in the **same unit as the mean** – how spread out observations are.

blocks.name: Mean, variance and standard deviation
blocks.note: Dispersion = how much a distribution is stretched or squeezed.

blocks.title: Five customers rate a product (1–5)
blocks.question: Compute mode, median and mean.
steps: Mode: 4 and 5 both occur twice → bimodal
blocks.result: Mean (3.8) < median (4): the single low rating pulls the mean down – the median is robust to outliers.

sections.heading: Bivariate analysis: correlation
sections.lead: Multivariate analysis looks at two (bivariate) or more variables – typically one dependent and several independent variables.

blocks.caption: r = 0 only means no **linear** relationship – there may still be a curved one. And even a strong r says nothing about causality.

blocks.title: Data analysis techniques in this course

items.label: Descriptive
items.text: Summarise a characteristic of a data set (univariate & bivariate).

items.label: Exploratory
items.text: Discover new connections – e.g. cluster analysis.

items.label: Causal
items.text: Relationships between variables and the impact of a change in one on another – regression.

blocks.title: In Stata (Superstore exercise)
blocks.text: Compute means/SDs for numerical variables, **frequencies** for categorical ones, **cross-tabs** for two categorical variables and **correlations** between metric ones – then ask: what can I conclude, and what would I recommend?

items.text: A key tool to make sense of and interact with massive data sets: present, navigate, aggregate and see details so that complex questions can be answered (visual analytics process, Keim et al., 2010).
Converting raw data into easily understood pictures of information that enable fast and effective decisions.

blocks.title: Five ways to organise information – “LATCH” hat racks (Wurman)

items.label: Location
items.text: Data from different sources or places (where goods are distributed)

items.label: Alphabet
items.text: Huge amounts of data or audiences unfamiliar with categories

items.label: Time
items.text: Events over fixed durations – changes are easy to compare

items.label: Category
items.text: Items of similar importance, goods and industries

items.label: Hierarchy
items.text: By magnitude – small to large, cheap to expensive, by importance

blocks.title: Which chart for which purpose?
head: Chart
Use it to …
Avoid when …
rows: Compare categories or change over time; show positive and negative values
Show relative proportions (part-to-whole) for one factor
Continuous data over time; several series on one timeline; trends rather than exact values
Part-to-whole relations plus the volume over time
Correlation and clustering; distribution; order of points irrelevant
Relation plus the size of a third phenomenon
Compare several features of one or more samples

blocks.title: Grammar for visual creation – a checklist for good (and against bad) charts

items.label: Data & statistics
items.text: Source given? Statistics accurate and complete (p-value, confidence interval)?

items.label: Aesthetics & position
items.text: Organised by a hat rack, obeys reading gravity, proper alignment and use of space.

items.label: Coordinates & geometry
items.text: Scale complete (not cut)? Shapes in proper scale and easy to compare?

items.label: Guides & theme
items.text: Not too many labels; colour-blind friendly (protan-, deuteran-, tritanopia).

items.label: Manipulation
items.text: Unbiased display, no illusory effects, no truncated axes to exaggerate.

items.label: Visual variables
items.text: Size, orientation (hierarchies), shape, colour (categories), value, texture.

recap: Scales: **nominal** (no order) → **ordinal** (order) → **interval** (equal steps, no true zero, e.g. Likert) → **ratio** (true zero, e.g. sales).
Mode works for all scales, the median from ordinal, mean/SD/correlation only for metric data.
Dichotomous & multiple choice → nominal; rank order → ordinal; Likert → interval.
Pearson r between −1 and +1 measures direction and strength of a **linear** relationship – not causality.
Choose charts by purpose: bars compare, lines show time, pies show shares (≤ 6–7), scatter shows relationships.
exam: T/F on measurement scales and which statistic is allowed (“The median can be computed for nominal variables” → false).
Small calculations: NPS, CSAT, CES from given response counts.
Interpretation of a correlation coefficient (sign, strength, no causality).
traps: NPS is a **difference of percentages**, not an average score – passives drop out.
Likert scales are treated as **interval**, not ordinal, in this course.
A correlation of 0 does not mean the variables are unrelated – only that there is no linear relation.
